strings.text: The Chrysalids

You are David Strorm, son of the strictest man in Waknuk. Here one toe too many is reason enough to cast a child out into the Fringes. You and your friends differ in a way no one can see: you speak to each other in thoughts. So far, no one knows.
In a community where any difference is a sin, a boy hides his gift: he hears his friends’ thoughts.
after the novel by John Wyndham
Six toes
How to speak to Sophie
“Does it hurt?”
“Whose are you?”
sit beside her
The rider on the meadow
covered it in time
too late
Mrs Wender’s look

I was ten. The sandy bank by the stream was all mine.
Until a girl got up out of the grass at the top.
Does it hurt?
Whose are you?
Sit beside her
Does it hurt?
It hurts. Only don’t look at it.
Whose are you? I haven’t seen you before.
The Wenders’. We live over the hill.
Untie it. Only carefully.
I sat down beside her and said nothing. She cried a little more, and was quiet.
There were six toes on her foot.
Every Sunday my father read us the Definitions: “And each foot shall have five toes.”
Hooves. Her foot must not be seen.
The rider went by and did not turn his head.
The rider reined in his horse. He looked at us from the meadow — a long time.
Then he rode on.
Promise you won’t tell anyone.
I promise
I promise.
Mummy!
Finger to lips
Look away
She nodded to me. As to a grown-up.
Mrs Wender will remember this.
I looked at the sand. When I raised my eyes, she was already going — quickly, without looking back.
Her name was Sophie. From that day on we met nearly every day.
All summer we ran off to the ruins of the Old People — where we were not allowed to go.
Something glinted in the grass. I began to scrape the earth away with my hands.
A smooth plate with the Old People’s letters on it. What had it been for?
Showing the way
For prayers
A toy
To show the way.
They prayed to it.
It’s just a toy.
Perhaps. Only the roads from here had led nowhere for a long time.
Hush. If they hear, we’ll be in trouble.
Some toys they had!
Take it home
Leave it
I pushed it inside my shirt.
Let it lie. The Old People knew so much — and lost it all the same.
From far off, from Waknuk, came the sound of the bell. Time to go home.
I never did dig it out all the way.
Grab it, run
Pull it, run
Drop it, run
Run home
At home it smelt of bread and wax.
Where have you been all day, David?
By the stream
About the girl
By the stream. On my own.
I met a girl. She has six toes on her foot.
Sophie will remember this.
Your father was asking. Don’t be late for prayers.
No one. Do you hear? Not your father, not the inspector. No one.
Sophie will not know of it. Not yet.
That night I hid the Old People’s plate under a floorboard.
As it should be
The evening chores
as it should be
lost the order
The cut hand
hold my hand out to my mother
“I can do it”
“If I had another hand”
say it again to my father
“Nothing, Father”
On my knees
look for my mother
look at the floor
The calf
tell my father
lead it behind the barn
On our knees with everyone
go down on my knees
be late
The hymn by the fire
sing at the top of my voice
move my lips
keep silent
The stalk on the ashes
stay by the stalk
go with my mother
The night before the raid
warn Sophie
stay at home
With my father everything was done as it should be. In the evening — water from the well, then the barn, then prayers.
Not now. First — water from the well.
Not now. First — the barn.
Now — prayers.
Draw water
Shut the barn
Go to prayers
My father saw it all. He said nothing — and that was the worst of it.
That evening I cut my hand open on the harrow.
When my father was reading, one came into the house on tiptoe.
Offer my hand
I’ll do it
I can do it.
Give it here.
That’s no way to tie it.
If I’d had another hand, I could have managed it myself.
What did you say?
Say it again
Nothing, Father
I said… if I had another hand…
This is the Image of God. One head. Two hands.
Lord, forgive him his word. Let him never wish for another image.
Raise my eyes
Look down
I looked at the floor. Only much later did I learn that she had looked at me then.
Go upstairs.
No one cleared away my bowl that evening.
Nothing, Father.
Emily. What did he say?
That his hand hurts, Joseph. That is all.
Mother will remember this.
My mother had never lied to my father before.
Every autumn the inspector came and decided what should live.
I watched our calf from behind the barn — until the inspector looked at it.
Tell my father
Its legs were a little too long. Only a little.
The inspector reached the calf before I did. Its legs were a little too long. Only a little.
Lead it away
Father, the calf’s legs aren’t right.
While the inspector leafed through his book, I led the calf away behind the barn.
The inspector found nothing. But the farmhand saw where I had taken it.
The farmhand will remember this.
I told. My father turned slowly towards me.
I kept quiet. The inspector saw it for himself.
You keep your eyes open. That is good, David.
Father will remember this.
They took the calf away. My father did not look my way.
They burned the deviant wheat till dawn, the whole community together. What was in doubt, the inspector decided.
An Offence.
Kneel
Everyone was on their knees already. Everyone but me.
The wheat caught at once, crackling like straw.
Everyone sang. You had to sing with everyone — in time.
David… Will they do that to us too? Into the fire?
Don’t sing with them. Please.
I sang loudly, louder than my mother. The voice was not mine.
I only moved my lips. My father was looking straight at us.
I did not sing. My father was looking straight at us.
By morning all that was left of the field was a grey strip.
Stay by it
Go with Mother
Don’t look over there, David. Come along.
I did not look back.
When my father was reading, you were not to stir.
I took hold of the edge of the table and kept still.
“And each leg shall have two joints and one foot, and each foot five toes…”
…and whatever is not so formed is a Blasphemy against the true Image, and hateful in the sight of God.
A rider saw the Wender girl by the stream. Barefoot.
The Wenders have a daughter with a Deviation. They’ll be fetched in the morning.
David? What’s wrong with you? You’re as tight as a string.
Sit still while the Word is read.
My mother did not raise her eyes. She knew whom he meant.
I looked at the table and counted my heartbeats.
Warn the Wenders
Stay in bed
I lay down without undressing.
I waited until the house was still.
They’ll come for you in the morning.
Mummy knows. We’re going to the Fringes.
Thank you, David.
In the morning the Wenders’ house stood empty.
I lay and listened to the rain.
Sophie will think you knew.
They were caught at the very edge of the Fringes. They said Sophie broke free and ran into the forest.
Voices
Uncle Axel asked
point to the window
shake my head
A strange voice
answer her
Rosalind on the square
look at her

Uncle Axel had been a sailor once. Then he hurt his leg and became my father’s smith.
I liked to sit on a barrel in his forge. And to chatter — with someone no one but me could hear.
David? Are you at the forge again?
Yes. Uncle’s making horseshoes. It’s warm here.
Our cow got loose. The whole house was out catching her.
I laughed out loud. My uncle’s hammer stopped.
Who are you talking to, Davie?
Show the window
Shake my head
Beyond the field the Mortons’ window was lit. That was where Rosalind lived.
Right across the field? Without words?
No one, eh? And yet you look — over there.
No one, do you hear? Not your father, not your mother. Not a living soul.
And tell the others the same.
Your father. To the bellows, Davie. Quick.
The farmhand had told him about the calf. My father was looking not at my uncle — at me.
My bellows wheezed out of time. My father raised his lantern and looked at me for a long while.
My father stood a while, nodded to my uncle and went away.
My uncle said nothing. He only nodded to me across the forge.
In the evenings my uncle told me what he had seen over the sea.
The sea?
The Old People?
The people there?
What is it like, the sea?
Have you seen where the Old People lived?
And what are the people like there?
Bigger than all our land. You sail for weeks — and not a shore in sight.
I have. Black glass for miles and miles. Nothing grows there to this day.
All sorts. In the south there’s a coast where everyone has six toes. And they think we’re the deviants.
Our ship was a tall one, three masts. Sails one above the other.
And over the glass — towers. Taller than our church tower, and every one of them broken.
Their coast is green. The trees are thin and tall, and their tops are like umbrellas.
I showed him the plate from the ruins.
Hide it. And don’t show it to your father.
I thought of Sophie.
The true image, you say? And who has ever seen it, this image?
Labrador isn’t the whole world, Davie.
The years went by. We found one another — those who could hear.
By day, at work, we learnt to know one another right across the valley.
Half the day at the washing line again. Is anybody there?
Anne.
Anne. She found me herself.
The sheep are scattered all over the hill. David, where are you?
The ploughman looked at me a long time from under his hand. And I stood and looked at the sky.
I went back to my hoeing. The ploughman stood a while and started his horse.
Michael. Then Mark answered — from a cart on the road.
Who’s there? Who is it talking?
Don’t answer. We don’t know her.
She’s all alone out there. As we were once.
Answer her
Keep quiet
I thought I was the only one.
Now there are nine of us. And nine of us who might let it slip.
Who’s there…?
She called for a few more evenings. Then she stopped.
We were sixteen. In front of everyone, Rosalind and I were almost strangers.
That day the old woman by the well never took her eyes off me.
My eyes went looking for her by themselves. I kept taking them away — to the well, to the church, anywhere.
Don’t look at me. Just listen.
Some day we’ll go away from here. The two of us.
Where to? It’s the Fringes all round.
Uncle says the world is bigger than Labrador.
Then — there.
I’m smiling now. A pity you can’t see.
Don’t. They’re looking at us.
The old woman with the stick watched us until we parted.
Rosalind will remember this.
I never did turn round. She went off with her parents without looking back.
Some day I want you to look at me. In front of everyone.
At night I went up the hill and called them. One after another.
I’m here.
Here. Why so late?
And me.
Suddenly an answer came from our own house — so thin and so loud my ears rang. And at once it was gone.
Then Sally and Katherine. Mark. Rachel.
Don’t call me any more. I’m marrying Alan Ervin.
I want to live like everyone else. Do you hear? Like everyone else.
She’ll tell him. Not at once — but in a year.
She’s one of us. You can’t hold her by force.
Let her go
Tell Axel
Then we’ll pray she keeps quiet.
Anne will remember this.
I told my uncle about Anne and Alan.
All right. Off to bed, Davie.
A week later Alan was found by the road. With an arrow in his throat.
My uncle asked me nothing. Nor I him.
It was you. I know it was you.
Anne answered no more.
And at home, in the little room, my sister Petra was asleep.
I did not know yet who had answered me from our house.
Petra
The cry at the river
she went quiet
she cried to the end

teach her to hide her thoughts
let her be herself
The voice from over the sea
answer
only listen
In spring, when Petra was six, she went off to the river alone.
And then it struck into my head. Not a voice — fear, enormous, without words.
David…!
Petra, I’m here. Breathe with me.
She went quiet. No one farther than Rosalind heard her.
The grown-ups heard not a sound. They saw her run.
I brought her out onto the bank. She was crying — out loud, like any child.
I brought her out onto the bank. She called to the very last — and not with her mouth.
Is that her? Your sister?
I held on. But the branch broke.
All of ours heard her. And they saw us running.
She went quiet all of a sudden. Was it you who calmed her?
She’s stronger than all of us, David. What are we going to do with her?
Carry Petra home
From that day Petra was among us. Her thoughts thundered all over the district.
Here. Quietly, David. She’s listening.
David, is that you? I want to be with you too!
She shouted us all down. Alone.
Anne has guessed already. Teach Petra to hide her thoughts, David.
Teach her to hide her thoughts. Or the wrong people will hear her.
We hide all our lives. Let her at least be as she is.
Hide her thoughts
Let her call
My father taught me to spot Deviations. Now I was teaching my sister to hide them.
Every evening I taught her: think quietly, very quietly, as if you were whispering.
All right. I’ll be tiny, tiny.
Petra will remember this.
David! I can hear all of you! All of you!
She’ll give us away, David.
Once already I had told myself to keep quiet. I did not want to again.
I dreamt of that city again. I followed a shining fish with my eyes — quietly, quietly, so as not to wake.
The dream fell apart. I never made out the towers.
I had time to make out every tower.
A month later Petra woke me in the middle of the night.
David, somebody’s talking out there. Far, far away, over the water.
She showed me what she saw. And I knew the city from my dream.
Who are you, little girl? Where are you? You call so loudly.
…who are you… where…
I can’t hear words. Only that somebody’s there.
Answer her, Petra
Don’t answer
Answer her, Petra.
Don’t answer. We don’t know who it is.
I’m Petra! I’m here!
I hear you. Call to me again.
David, what is it? Someone strange can hear us.
Petra did as she was told. The voice called a while longer, fainter and fainter, and then it was gone.
That city was real. Somewhere over the sea.
I never did know whether it was a dream.

That evening my father read longer than usual.
Anne is dead. She left a letter for the inspector. All our names are in it.
Anne told Alan everything. In the morning Alan was at the inspector’s.
We’ve been given away.
They’ve taken Katherine and Sally. They’re being questioned.
David… They’re asking about you. I won’t tell. I’ll try.
David. What are you thinking about while I read?
He’s tired, Joseph. Let him go to bed.
Go tonight. With Petra. Rosalind will wait at the ford.
Go with Petra
Free the girls
Then I’ll wait at the ford. Till dawn — no longer.
Katherine and Sally will remember this.
In the night I woke Petra and carried her out of the house.
David, where are we going?
Far away. Only think quietly.
I can’t do quietly!
Look back
Don’t look back
My mother stood at the window. She watched us go, and she did not call my father.
The window went dark. No one in the house woke.
Riders were waiting at the gate. The inspector knew whom to come for.
Petra, run to the ford. To Rosalind.
Petra slipped out of my arms and vanished into the dark. No one went after her.
I hear her. I’m coming to meet her.
I ran to Uncle Axel. There was no one else to go to.
They’re holding them at the inspector’s, in the cellar. The door’s locked.
I’ll make a key. And you work the bellows — let them think I’m working.
A man with a lantern stopped in the gateway.
My father’s farmhand. The one who saw the calf.
Work the bellows
Nod to strike
He looked me in the face — and whistled. Two more came up out of the dark.
My uncle stood there with his hammer. I shook my head: don’t.
He stood a while and went away. He did not notice. Or did not want to.
My uncle stepped towards the gate. The man had no time to turn round.
We dragged him into the dark. He was breathing.
Towards morning my uncle came back alone.
They’re away. Another road, to the Fringes. Now it’s your turn, Davie.
They brought me to the meeting-house. It was night; one lamp burned on the elders’ table.
The men came in one by one and sat down along the walls. My father stood apart.
The girls named you, David. Do you hear them without words?
I don’t understand
Keep silent
I hear them
I don’t understand what you mean.
I do. And there is no sin in it.
They didn’t understand at first either.
Answer when you are asked.
Then you are no son of mine.
In the morning they’ll take you away. They’ll ask you differently there.
David. We’re close. Now.
Someone shouted in the yard: the barn was on fire.
Everyone rushed for the doors — the inspector, my father, the men.
Petra’s with us — we got her out through the window. Run to the ford.
Petra’s with me. Run to the ford.
Run
There are too few of us, David. Get yourself out.
Blow it out
Knock it over
In the dark my father caught me by the sleeve. I tore free.
He shouted after me until I reached the gate.
The oil flared up across the floor. Everyone rushed to put it out, and I made for the window.
I carried Petra out through the window of her room.
I took Sheba from the paddock behind the house. Petra was already waiting for me — in a pannier on Rosalind’s horse.
David! I knew you’d come!
Rosalind was waiting beyond the ford, on the ridge, with her father’s two great-horses.
I’m staying. I’ll be among them — and I’ll listen.
Let her go, David. She’s no match for the great-horses. And she neighs fit to wake the whole district.
Let Sheba go
Take Sheba
Sheba went home alone. There was no way back.
I couldn’t. I led her back and tied her rein to the pack-horse.
Lanterns on the road. Your father is with them.
They found that man at the forge. The whole district has turned out after you.
Beyond the shoulder of the ridge the road dipped into a hollow. The hollow was full of fog.
We stand still. Let them go by.
Two riders with lanterns came up onto the crest.
The first one raised his lantern higher — and saw us. The second galloped back for the others.
He’s coming this way.
They shone their lanterns into the fog for a long time. Then the second turned back for the others, and the first stayed to watch the road.
It’ll be dawn soon. The fog will lift — and he’ll see us.
Shoot him
Over his head
Freeze
Shoot him.
Shoot over his head!
I had no time to say anything. Rosalind had already drawn her bow.
The rider fell. His horse went off over the crest alone.
He wouldn’t have spared us, David.
He never saw us at all.
The arrow whistled just over his head. The horse shied, and the rider galloped off over the crest.
He saw where we went.
Now he knows where we are.
We froze. Petra clapped her little hand over her mouth.
He rode right up to the edge of the hollow and shone his lantern into the fog for a long time.
He rode along the edge of the hollow, shining his lantern into the fog. Very close.
He saw us. He won’t come back alone.
We’ve lost an hour. Now they’ll reach the Fringes before us.
By dawn the lanterns had fallen behind. By day we hid in the woods.
They’ve taken Katherine and Sally away. I could do nothing.
That rider died. There’ll be no mercy now — not for you, not for them.
We hear you. Hold on. We are coming.
David, that lady over the water is calling again. She’s looking for us.
On the second night we came out to the last field. Beyond the fence the Fringes began.
The lantern was carried by a tall man. I knew my father by his walk.
The moon stood behind the woods, and the shadows of the trees lay across the field. We could walk along them — or while he shone his light the other way.
There they are! By the fence!
There they are! In the field!
Behind us there was shouting, lanterns running to the fence. But no one stepped over it.
The lantern stood a while by the fence and turned back.
That’s it, David. We’re in the Fringes.
The deviant forest closed behind us.
The Fringes
Sophie by the hut
go up to her
wait by the fire
Sophie
hid us
told whose son I am
The Spider-man
stand with the Fringes
go to the cave
We were brought to the fire. The people round it were not like us. And not like the people in Waknuk.
They knew already that we had been followed right to the fence.
By the farthest hut stood a girl in a faded headscarf. Barefoot.
Do you know her?
Go to Sophie
Wait here
I went up to her. She did not step back.
I stayed by the fire. She watched me across the whole camp.
David. I remember you.
You came running that night. We got away in time.
Come into my hut. Before he’s back.
Sophie hid you.
Until evening she let no one near us.
That’s Strorm’s son. Joseph Strorm’s.
Sophie did not forget.
Rosalind and Petra were tied to a post. I was taken to the one who decided things here.
David, the rope’s prickly!
In the evening a tall man came out to the fire, with long arms like a spider’s.
He looked me over for a long time. Then he said he was my father’s brother.
We’re here, David, Katherine and I. They leave us alone while they need us.
Your father is leading them here. You hear each other without words — you’ll be my eyes.
Stand with us — and I’ll let your people go.
He’s just like your father, David. Only from the other side.
Stand with them
Untie my own
To the cave
He nodded, and the ropes at the post were cut.
They put us by the cave above the clearing. From there you could see where they would come from.
In the night the fire burned low. I crawled to the post and cut the ropes.
Sophie saw. She turned away to the fire.
In the night Sophie led us out of the camp by a path even the sentries did not know.
There was nowhere further to run. We hid in the cave above the clearing.
At dawn a horn sounded.
They were coming on our tracks — from that same fence.
They were coming through the forest. Many of them. With guns.
Your father is in front. I can hear him — not in words, I just know.
David! She’s very close! She says — keep together!
We are almost over you. Don’t scatter. A little longer.
I call her and call her… She hears, but she can’t find us.
Petra was silent. No one called her from over the sea.
Sophie ran to where the Spider-man had gone.
Sealand
The return
Stayed with Michael
Alone
The city of my dream turned out to be real. No one there counted toes.
But even there they spoke of people of the old kind the way my father spoke of Deviations.
Eight years later I came back to Waknuk. Unarmed.
Michael was waiting at the ford. They listened to us. Not all of them — but they listened.
The ship went away. We stayed on the ledge — Rosalind, Michael and I.
What came next was for us to decide now.
Rosalind flew away with Petra. I stayed with Michael.
At night I listened to the sky. Sometimes it answered.
The ship never came. We stayed by the Fringes.
A year later Petra stopped calling. And I stopped waiting.
My father fell
run to him
stay

cover Petra
cover Rosalind
shield my father
fall beside him

fly away

We lay behind a rock by the cave. Down below, on the clearing, there was shooting.
We told the Spider-man where they were coming from. Too late to be sorry now.
Your father. In front, by the horse.
Run to Father
Stay
You can’t, David! You can’t help him!
Sophie was running to the Spider-man.
David! Stop!
Don’t touch me.
Go, David. Get away from here.
We waited for the ship. The sky stayed empty.
The Waknuk men faltered and ran for the forest. They left my father behind.
David… She doesn’t answer any more.
It’s her! David, it’s her!
Shield my father
Fall beside him
Cover Petra
Cover Rosalind
Petra lay very still under me. The threads settled on my back.
Rosalind held Petra. I held them both.
I reached no one in time. The threads settled on everyone.
I lay over my father. The threads settled on me, not on him.
I fell beside him. The threads settled on us both.
They were soft and sticky. And the more you struggled, the tighter they held.
It grew quiet. The ship came down in the middle of the clearing.
It’s you! I know you!
So this is what you are like, Petra. How loudly you call.
David! Are you alive? I can hardly hear you.
Brave. And foolish.
Under the threads my father was breathing. I saw his fingers stir.
This one I will not free. He came to kill you.
Don’t pity them. Their time is over.
I’m staying, David. Someone has to tell our kind that we exist.
Fly away
Stay with Michael
David, where are you going? Are you coming with us?
Where you go — I go.
I can’t stay, David. Not here. Not after all this.
Come, David.
On the threshold I looked back. Once.
I’ll tell them. Some day they’ll begin to listen.
